questions.q:
Assertion (A): After 1008 Mahmud had easy access to the Indus plains and the lands beyond.
Reason (R): The Hindu Shahis, who had resisted earlier invasions, had now been overrun by the Ghaznavids.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The Shahis had held the way in from the Khyber Pass side, so once they were overrun and Anandapala was overcome the route into the Indus plains lay open. R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Aman writes, 'In 1018 Mahmud sacked Mathura, and he was then already 58 years old.' Using the year and age of his death given in the chapter, show that this cannot be right, and say how old he was in 1018.
questions.a: Mahmud died in 1030 at the age of 58. In 1018 he was 12 years younger, so 58 - 12 = 46 years old. If he had been 58 in 1018, he would have been 70 at his death, which the chapter does not say.
s: Recalls death in 1030 at the age of 58
Shows that 58 in 1018 would make him 70 in 1030, so the claim is impossible
States the correct age, 46, in 1018

questions.q:
A textbook committee is choosing two quotations about Mahmud for a classroom display. Quotation X, from a scholar who travelled with his army: 'The Hindu Shahiya dynasty is now extinct ... they never slackened in the ardent desire of doing that which is good and right.' Quotation Y, from his court historian: 'Wherever he went, Mahmud plundered and sacked the country until it was annihilated ... destroying their temples ... built mosques instead.'
(a) Name the scholar who wrote Quotation X and the region (now in Uzbekistan) he came from.
(b) What does Quotation X tell us about the writer's attitude, given where he stood?
(c) Which two aims of Mahmud does Quotation Y point to?
(d) A student proposes to display only Quotation Y and write 'Plunder was the only reason for the raids'. Using Quotation Y and what the chapter says about larger temples, judge this proposal.
questions.a: (a) Al-Biruni, from Khwarizm. (b) The writer, though in Mahmud's entourage, spoke of the defeated dynasty with respect. (c) Plunder and spreading his version of Islam (destroying temples and building mosques). (d) The proposal is weak. Larger temples held immense wealth from centuries of offerings, so plunder was a real motive, but Quotation Y itself speaks of destroying temples and building mosques, pointing to spreading Islam. The word 'only' is therefore too strong.
s: Part (a): al-Biruni, from Khwarizm
Part (b): respect for the defeated dynasty from a writer on the conqueror's side
Part (c): plunder and spreading his version of Islam
Part (d): uses Quotation Y and the wealth of larger temples to reject 'only'

questions.q: Why does the chapter say the resistance of the Hindu Shahis 'made a difference'?
questions.a: They controlled the Khyber Pass, one of the main passes through the Hindu Kush that invaders used to enter the Subcontinent. The other options attach the Shahis to places or routes the chapter gives to other powers.
o: They controlled the Khyber Pass in the Hindu Kush
They controlled the Strait of Malacca on the China trade route
They held the port of Somnath on the coast of Saurashtra
They held the hills near Mount Abu that guard Gujarat

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the chapter about Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns?
questions.a: The chapter says he did not try to set up a permanent base in India beyond Punjab, so he did not rule the Gangetic plains from Mathura. The other three are given in the text.
o: He ruled the Ganga plains from a new capital, Mathura
He returned to Ghazni with huge booty after each campaign
His army used horse-mounted archers in daring attacks
The Chandellas of central India resisted him strongly

questions.q:
Match each event of Mahmud's career in Column A with its year in Column B.
Column A: 1. Overcame Anandapala after a long battle  2. Sacked the wealthy city of Mathura  3. Destroyed the Somnath temple  4. Died at Ghazni
Column B: a. 1018  b. 1030  c. 1026  d. 1008
questions.a: Anandapala was overcome in 1008, Mathura was sacked in 1018, Somnath fell in 1026 and Mahmud died in 1030. The wrong pairings swap the two raids (1018 and 1026) or put his death earlier.

questions.q: Dev says, 'This chapter should skip the destruction and killing of Mahmud's raids so that nobody feels bad.' Using the 'word of caution' at the start of the chapter's account, do you agree?
questions.a: No. The chapter says history has often recorded war and destruction more than peace, and that it is better to face dark periods and analyse them to understand what made them possible and help avoid recurrence. It also adds that it is wrong to hold anyone responsible today for past events.
s: Verdict: disagrees, the darker periods should be faced
Reason: analysing them shows what made them possible and helps avoid recurrence
Adds that nobody today is to be held responsible for past events

questions.q: (a) What did the court historian al-Utbi say about the temple that overlooked Mathura? (b) What kind of place was Somnath when Mahmud reached it, and where does the chapter place it?
questions.a: (a) He wrote that even the pens of all writers and the pencils of all painters would be unable to describe the temple's beauty and decoration. (b) A bustling seaport, in Saurashtra (Gujarat).
s: Part (a): pens of all writers and pencils of all painters could not describe its beauty and decoration
Part (b): a bustling seaport in Saurashtra

questions.q: What is meant by the title 'sultan'? Name the Ghaznavid ruler who conquered the Hindu Shahis and took this title.
questions.a: 'Sultan' is a word of Arabic origin meaning authority or power; in the Muslim world it came to mean a sovereign ruler or king. Mahmud of Ghazni took the title.
s: Gives the meaning authority or power, a sovereign ruler
Names Mahmud of Ghazni

questions.q: 'Mahmud's campaigns met resistance only from the Hindu Shahis.' Justify or refute this statement using at least three examples from the chapter.
questions.a: The statement is false. The Hindu Shahis did resist, and Anandapala fought a long battle in 1008 with help from several north Indian rulers. But the Chandellas of central India also resisted strongly and Mahmud was close to defeat a few times, and at Somnath the locals resisted strongly and his army suffered severe losses before he gained the upper hand. So resistance came from several quarters; Mahmud's rapid marches and daring cavalry with mounted archers were ultimately decisive.
s: Verdict: refutes the statement as too narrow
The Shahis' long battle in 1008 with support from other rulers
The Chandellas' strong resistance and Mahmud being close to defeat
Somnath: strong local resistance and severe losses to his army
Concludes that rapid marches and cavalry still decided the outcome

questions.q: The word 'sultan', which Mahmud of Ghazni took as his title, is of Arabic origin. What does it mean in the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says it means 'authority' or 'power', and that in the Muslim world it came to refer to a sovereign ruler or king. The other meanings are not given by the book.

questions.q: (a) Name the dynasty that controlled the Khyber Pass before the Ghaznavids overran it, and say what else the pass was used for, apart from invasions, for at least 2,500 years. (b) A Ghaznavid ruler wants to reach the Indus plains from Ghazni. Why must he first deal with that dynasty?
questions.a: (a) The Hindu Shahis; the pass was a major trade route connecting the Subcontinent to Central Asia and the route Buddhist scholars and monks travelled. (b) The Shahis held the pass through which invaders entered the Subcontinent, so the way into the Indus plains lay through their territory; the Ghaznavids had to overrun them first.
s: Part (a): Hindu Shahis, and the pass as a trade route and a route for Buddhist scholars and monks
Part (b): invaders entered through this pass, so controlling it made resistance count

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Ghaznavid invasions.
1. Mahmud conducted 17 campaigns in India.
2. In 1008 Anandapala defeated Mahmud because several rulers of north India helped him.
3. Salar Masud, according to oral history and a 17th-century chronicle, fell in battle against Suheldev at Bahraich.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: Mahmud overcame Anandapala in 1008 despite the help Anandapala received from other north Indian rulers.

questions.q: Describe how Mahmud of Ghazni overcame the Hindu Shahis and then raided deeper into India, and explain why the chapter treats his campaigns as raids and not as the founding of a lasting rule.
questions.a: The Shahis held the Khyber Pass and resisted with the help of other Indian rulers. Mahmud defeated Jayapala and, in 1008, Jayapala's son Anandapala after a long battle in northern Punjab, which opened the Indus plains. He sacked Mathura in 1018, looted Kannauj and destroyed Somnath in 1026. In all he made 17 campaigns and returned to Ghazni with booty each time. He did not attempt a permanent base beyond Punjab, so the campaigns were raids.
s: Shahis, the Khyber Pass and the defeat of Jayapala
1008 victory over Anandapala despite help from other rulers
Mathura, Kannauj and Somnath named with the kind of damage done
17 campaigns, each ending with a return to Ghazni with booty
No permanent base beyond Punjab, so raids and not lasting rule

questions.q: (a) Give two reasons from the chapter why Mahmud's army was ultimately decisive even when it met strong resistance. (b) Name one group of central India that resisted him.
questions.a: (a) Its rapid marches and its daring cavalry attacks with archers on horseback. (b) The Chandellas.
s: Part (a): rapid marches and daring cavalry attacks with mounted archers
Part (b): Chandellas of central India

questions.q: Who was Salar Masud? How does the chapter say his attack on the Gangetic region ended, and what are its sources?
questions.a: Mahmud's nephew. At Bahraich the local ruler Suheldev resisted and Salar Masud fell in the battle; the sources are oral history and a 17th-century Muslim chronicle.
s: Salar Masud as Mahmud's nephew who attacked the Gangetic region
Suheldev stopped him at Bahraich, based on oral history and a 17th-century chronicle

questions.q: Nisha reads that a ruler fought a campaign every few years, took back wealth and prisoners to his own capital each time, and set up no lasting base beyond one province. Which description from the chapter fits him best?
questions.a: Mahmud returned to Ghazni with booty after each of 17 campaigns and did not build a base beyond Punjab, which makes his campaigns repeated raids. Muhammad Ghuri is the contrast: he sought territorial conquest and left commanders behind.
o: Mahmud of Ghazni, whose campaigns were repeated raids
Muhammad Ghuri, who left Aibak to rule Delhi
Prithviraj III, who held Delhi and Ajmer for his own kingdom
Bakhtiyar Khilji, who took Bihar and Bengal for the Ghurids

questions.q:
The history club of a Pune school is making a timeline poster on Mahmud's campaigns. The draft entries read: 'A long battle in northern Punjab, 1008'; 'A wealthy city of western Uttar Pradesh whose temple overlooked it, 1018, followed by Kannauj'; 'A bustling seaport of Saurashtra, 1026'; 'Died at Ghazni aged 58, 1030'.
(a) Name the city of the second entry and the temple of the third.
(b) Which dynasty did Mahmud overcome in the first entry, and what did that victory give him?
(c) Name two things, besides plunder of treasure, that his campaigns involved.
(d) The club must choose a title: 'The Ghaznavid Raids' or 'The Ghaznavid Conquest'. Decide which title the entries and one fact in the chapter support better, and say why the other fits less well.
questions.a: (a) Mathura; the Somnath (Somanatha Shiva) temple. (b) The Hindu Shahis (Anandapala, son of Jayapala); the victory gave him easy access to the Indus plains and beyond. (c) Destruction of temples, killing of tens of thousands of civilians and capture of prisoners, including children, sold on slave markets of Central Asia. (d) 'Raids' fits better: he returned to Ghazni after each of 17 campaigns and set up no permanent base beyond Punjab. 'Conquest' fits only the overrunning of the Shahis, so it overstates the rest.
s: Part (a): Mathura and the Somnath temple
Part (b): Hindu Shahis, and easy access to the Indus plains
Part (c): two of destruction, slaughter of civilians, capture and sale of prisoners
Part (d): prefers Raids with the return-to-Ghazni / no-base fact and explains why Conquest fits less

questions.q: Historians have debated why Mahmud destroyed temples. Explain the debate by giving one point each from: what he did not do in India, what larger temples held, and what a contemporary writer noted.
questions.a: He did not try to set up a permanent base beyond Punjab, so many historians suggest plunder was the chief reason. Larger temples held immense wealth built up from devotees' offerings, so they were prime targets. But al-Utbi noted that he destroyed temples and built mosques, which shows Mahmud was also keen to spread his version of Islam.
s: No permanent base beyond Punjab, so plunder is suggested
Large temples held immense wealth from offerings and were prime targets
Al-Utbi's remark shows the aim of spreading his version of Islam

questions.q: A visitor to a museum reads that a Persian scholar who travelled with Mahmud wrote of the Hindu Shahis: 'in all their grandeur, they never slackened in the ardent desire of doing that which is good and right'. What can be concluded from this?
questions.a: A man from the invader's own entourage could write with respect about the defeated dynasty. He also calls the house extinct, so it does not show that the Shahis still ruled.
o: Even a writer in the conqueror's camp praised the Shahis
The writer was a minister who served the Hindu Shahi court
The Hindu Shahis were still ruling Punjab when he wrote this
The writer composed this remark before Jayapala was defeated

questions.q: How did Bhaskaracharya make his writings enjoyable and useful to both scholars and students?
questions.a: He used his gift for poetry. His works were full of examples, with clear explanations, demonstrations and proofs.
s: Poetry used to make the writing enjoyable
Examples with clear explanations, demonstrations and proofs

questions.q:
A school magazine in Lucknow is preparing a page on a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who came to India around 1017 with an army. The editor has two pieces of material: his encyclopaedic survey of India, and one sentence in which he says that the ruler he accompanied 'utterly ruined the prosperity of the country' and that Indian sciences 'fled to places which our hand cannot yet reach'. She must choose one heading for the page: 'An enemy's account of India', 'A scholar who studied India and recorded its losses', or 'A silent witness of the raids'.
(a) Name the scholar and the ruler he accompanied.
(b) Name two things he did to learn about India before writing the survey.
(c) What did he note about the effect of the ruler's campaigns, and where did the sciences go?
(d) Choose one heading and justify it using the survey and the sentence; say why one other heading fits less well.
questions.a: (a) Al-Biruni and Mahmud of Ghazni. (b) Any two of: learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts, conversed with Indian scholars. (c) He noted that Mahmud ruined the country's prosperity and that Indian sciences retired far from the conquered parts to places such as Kashmir and Varanasi. (d) 'A scholar who studied India and recorded its losses' fits best: the survey shows serious study of Indian religion, philosophy, sciences and more, and the sentence shows he openly recorded the damage. 'Enemy's account' ignores the survey and his respect for the Shahis; 'silent witness' is wrong because he wrote at length and spoke plainly.
s: Part (a): al-Biruni and Mahmud of Ghazni
Part (b): two of learning Sanskrit, reading texts, talking with scholars
Part (c): ruined prosperity; sciences moved to Kashmir, Varanasi and other places
Part (d): picks the scholar heading, justifies with survey and sentence, and rejects one other

questions.q: Describe three signs from the chapter that Bhaskaracharya's influence was long-lasting and reached beyond his own time.
questions.a: Many later scholars wrote commentaries on his works. Several were translated into Persian in the Mughal period. Europe took a few centuries to rediscover some of his pioneering techniques.
s: Later commentaries by many scholars
Persian translations in the Mughal period
Europe's rediscovery of some techniques a few centuries later

questions.q: Write a riddle in the style of Lilavati about peacocks in a Jaipur fort garden whose answer is a whole number, and solve it.
questions.a: Any valid riddle that can be solved, for example: 'A third of the peacocks were dancing, a sixth sat on the wall, and 9 were drinking at the fountain. How many peacocks?' A third and a sixth make a half, so 9 is the other half and the flock is 18.
s: A riddle in a story or verse style with clear numbers
The riddle can be solved to a whole number
The working and the final answer are correct

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT done by al-Biruni, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Lilavati was written by Bhaskaracharya, born in 1114, while al-Biruni came to India around 1017. The other three are credited to al-Biruni.
o: Writing the book Lilavati with riddles for students
Comparing Indian achievements with Greek and Islamic ones
Compiling the work of Aryabhata and Brahmagupta

questions.q: Which of Bhaskaracharya's works deals with more advanced algebra?
questions.a: Bijaganita is the algebra text. Lilavati teaches basic mathematics through riddles, Siddhantashiromani covers mathematical astronomy, and the Yogasutras are by Patanjali.

questions.q: A scholar from Khwarizm reaches India around 1017 and wants to understand Indian astronomy from its own books. What did al-Biruni do, according to the chapter?
questions.a: He learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and talked with Indian scholars. The Persian translations of Bhaskaracharya came in the Mughal period, and Lilavati was composed long after 1017.
o: Learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and talked with scholars
Read a Persian translation of Lilavati from Mahmud's library
Asked Bhaskaracharya to explain Siddhantashiromani to him
Relied on Greek summaries and wrote without Indian books

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bhaskaracharya's writings were favourite texts of students for centuries.
Reason (R): Siddhantashiromani deals with advanced astronomical calculations.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. But the reason does not explain the assertion: the chapter says the works were favourites because of their examples, clear explanations, demonstrations and proofs, and his gift for poetry.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Kiran wants to teach fractions to her Class 7 friends through verse riddles about elephants and lotus ponds, the way a 12th-century scholar did. Which work should she study as her model?
questions.a: Lilavati uses lively riddles and problems to teach basic mathematics, with the elephant-herd problem as an example. Bijaganita is advanced algebra and Siddhantashiromani is astronomy.

questions.q: 'Al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud's army, yet he studied India seriously.' Support this statement with five points from the chapter.
questions.a: He was a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who accompanied Mahmud around 1017. Even so, he learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and conversed with Indian scholars. His encyclopaedic survey covered Indian religion, philosophy, literature, geography and sciences and compared them with Greek and Islamic traditions. He compiled the work of Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta and translated Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic. He also recorded candidly how Mahmud's campaigns had harmed India's sciences.
s: His background: a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who accompanied Mahmud around 1017
Learning Sanskrit, reading texts and talking with Indian scholars
The survey and its comparison with Greek and Islamic traditions
Compiling Indian mathematics and astronomy and translating the Yogasutras
Recording how Mahmud's campaigns affected Indian sciences

questions.q: (a) Name the three famous works of Bhaskaracharya. (b) A Class 7 student wants a book that teaches basic mathematics through lively riddles. Which of the three suits her, and why?
questions.a: (a) Lilavati, Bijaganita and Siddhantashiromani. (b) Lilavati, because it uses lively riddles and problems to teach basic mathematics, while the other two are advanced algebra and mathematical astronomy.
s: Part (a): Lilavati, Bijaganita and Siddhantashiromani
Part (b): Lilavati, with the reason that it teaches basics through riddles

questions.q: During which period were several of Bhaskaracharya's works translated into Persian?
questions.a: The chapter says several were translated into Persian during the Mughal period. The Ghaznavid age is the look-alike, because al-Biruni's world was Persian-speaking, but the translations came later.

questions.q: (a) Name three Indian scholars whose mathematics and astronomy al-Biruni compiled. (b) Which classic text on yoga did he translate into Arabic?
questions.a: (a) Any three of Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta (the chapter says 'among others'). (b) Patanjali's Yogasutras.
s: Part (a): names Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta
Part (b): Patanjali's Yogasutras

questions.q: What subjects did al-Biruni's survey of India cover, and with which traditions did he often compare Indian achievements?
questions.a: It covered Indian religion, philosophy, literature, geography and sciences. He often compared them with those of the Greek and Islamic traditions.
s: Names the subjects of the survey
Greek and Islamic traditions as the comparison

questions.q: In which languages did al-Biruni write his many works?
questions.a: The chapter says he wrote prolifically in Arabic and Persian. He learned Sanskrit to read Indian texts, but did not write his own books in it.

questions.q: Ritu says, 'Al-Biruni's remark shows that Indian sciences retreated from the parts Mahmud conquered, but it does not show that Indian science came to an end.' Is she right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Al-Biruni said the sciences retired from the conquered parts to places such as Kashmir and Varanasi, so they moved rather than ended. The chapter adds that scientific knowledge declined in north India only a little later and continued to flourish in other regions, as in Bhaskaracharya (born 1114), whose Lilavati dates to about 1150. Her claim is right as stated; it would be wrong only if stretched to 'all Indian science continued everywhere'.
s: Verdict: agrees, the sciences moved and did not end
Al-Biruni's own words name Kashmir and Varanasi
Bhaskaracharya as evidence of continued flourishing, and the limit of the claim

questions.q: What did al-Biruni say had happened to Indian sciences in the parts of the country Mahmud conquered, and to which places did they move?
questions.a: He said they retired far away from the conquered parts and fled to places Mahmud's hand could not yet reach: Kashmir, Varanasi and other places.
s: Sciences retired from the conquered regions
Kashmir, Varanasi and other places named

questions.q: Compare al-Biruni and Bhaskaracharya on their homeland, their languages, their main works and what each contributed to the learning of the age.
questions.a: Al-Biruni was a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who wrote in Arabic and Persian; Bhaskaracharya was born in 1114, probably in present-day Maharashtra, and wrote in Sanskrit. Al-Biruni's main work was a survey of India; Bhaskaracharya's were Lilavati, Bijaganita and Siddhantashiromani. Al-Biruni gathered, compared and translated existing knowledge, while Bhaskaracharya advanced mathematics and astronomy with pioneering techniques in works that students loved for centuries.
s: Homeland of each scholar
Language of writing for each
Main works of al-Biruni
Main works of Bhaskaracharya
Contrast between recording and comparing existing knowledge, and advancing it

questions.q:
Read the following statements about two scholars of the age.
1. Al-Biruni was a mathematician, astronomer, geographer, historian and linguist.
2. He translated Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic.
3. Bhaskaracharya was born in 1114, probably in present-day Maharashtra.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are from the chapter: al-Biruni's many fields, his Arabic translation of the Yogasutras and Bhaskaracharya's birth year and probable birthplace.

questions.q:
A maths club in Nagpur has 22 members and is studying a 12th-century Sanskrit book that teaches basic mathematics through lively riddles. For next term it can buy only one more work by the same author. A survey shows that 14 members want to go on to more advanced algebra and 5 members want to learn advanced astronomical calculations; the other 3 have no preference.
(a) Name the book the club is studying and its author.
(b) Name the author's other two famous works and say what each deals with.
(c) Several of these works were translated into Persian in a later period. Name the period and say what it shows about the author.
(d) Which work should the club buy? Decide using the survey figures and the subject of each work.
questions.a: (a) Lilavati by Bhaskaracharya. (b) Bijaganita, on more advanced algebra; and Siddhantashiromani ('Crown of Treatises on Mathematical Astronomy'), on advanced astronomical calculations. (c) The Mughal period; it shows his influence was long-lasting in India and beyond. (d) Bijaganita: 14 of 22 members (the majority) want advanced algebra, against only 5 for astronomy, and Bijaganita is the work on advanced algebra.
s: Part (a): Lilavati by Bhaskaracharya
Part (b): Bijaganita (advanced algebra) and Siddhantashiromani (astronomical calculations)
Part (c): Mughal period, showing long-lasting influence
Part (d): Bijaganita, justified by 14 of 22 against 5 and the work's subject

questions.q: The chapter says that while north India bore the brunt of the Ghaznavid raids, the scene in eastern India was 'very different'. Using the two eastern dynasties named in the chapter's account, explain how it was different.
questions.a: In eastern India the chapter describes the rise and flourishing of local dynasties rather than Ghaznavid raids. The Senas became the dominant power in Bengal after the Palas, with their capital at Nadiya. The Eastern Gangas of Kalinga became one of the most stable powers of eastern India by the end of the 12th century, and began the Puri and Konark temples.
s: North India faced the raids, but the chapter's eastern story is of local dynasties
The Senas became dominant in Bengal after the Palas
The Eastern Gangas as a stable power that began major temples

questions.q: Where was the kingdom of the Eastern Gangas, and what do their inscriptions claim about its extent by the end of the 12th century?
questions.a: It was in Kalinga, more or less present-day Odisha. Their inscriptions claim it extended from the Ganga to the Godavari, which made them one of the most stable powers of eastern India.
s: Kalinga, more or less present-day Odisha
Extent from the Ganga to the Godavari by the end of the 12th century

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Senas are remembered as patrons of Hindu thought and literature.
Reason (R): Jayadeva, the author of the Gitagovindam, was hosted by the Palas.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true because the Senas hosted poets such as Jayadeva. R is false because Jayadeva was hosted by the Senas, while the Palas patronised Buddhist institutions.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Which poet, hosted by the Senas, wrote the Gitagovindam about Krishna and Radha?
questions.a: Jayadeva wrote the Gitagovindam at the Sena court. Merutunga recorded a battle in Gujarat, and al-Utbi and Minhaj al-Siraj Juzjani were chroniclers of the invaders.

questions.q: Write a quiz question whose answer is 'Vengi', and give a model answer of two sentences that uses facts from the chapter.
questions.a: For example: 'Which fertile region became the object of fierce wars between the Cholas and the Western Chalukyas?' Model answer: Vengi was the capital of the Eastern Chalukyas. As they were absorbed into the Chola sphere through marriage alliances, the region was fought over, and the Western Chalukyas faded.
s: A question that points only to Vengi
A model answer with a correct fact about Vengi's region or rulers
A second correct linked fact about the wars or the result

questions.q:
Match each dynasty in Column A with the detail in Column B.
Column A: 1. Senas  2. Eastern Gangas  3. Western Chalukyas  4. Eastern Chalukyas
Column B: a. ruled from Kalyani  b. had their capital at Vengi  c. ruled from Nadiya  d. began the Jagannatha temple at Puri
questions.a: The Senas ruled from Nadiya, the Eastern Gangas began the Jagannatha temple, the Western Chalukyas ruled from Kalyani and the Eastern Chalukyas had Vengi as capital. The wrong options swap the two Chalukya lines or the Senas and the Gangas.

questions.q: Explain how the political scene in Bengal changed after the decline of the Palas and what the change meant for religion and literature.
questions.a: After the Palas declined the Senas emerged as the dominant power over much of Bengal, with their capital at Nadiya, in the present Nadia district. Their relations with Kamarupa and Kalinga alternated between friendly and conflictual. The Palas had patronised Buddhist institutions, while the Senas promoted Hindu thought and literature. They hosted poets such as Jayadeva, who wrote the Gitagovindam about Krishna and Radha.
s: Senas emerging as dominant after the Palas
Capital Nadiya, in Nadia district
Alternating relations with Kamarupa and Kalinga
Palas patronised Buddhist institutions, Senas Hindu thought and literature
Jayadeva and the Gitagovindam as an example

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of the Eastern Gangas, as the chapter describes them?
questions.a: The Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur was built under Rajaraja Chola, not the Eastern Gangas. The Gangas began the Jagannatha temple at Puri and the Konark Sun temple.
o: They built the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur
They initiated the Jagannatha temple at Puri
They had marriage alliances with the Cholas
Their kingdom was said to stretch from the Ganga to the Godavari

questions.q: (a) Name the capital of the Senas and the region they dominated. (b) What does the chapter say about their relations with their neighbours Kamarupa and Kalinga?
questions.a: (a) Nadiya (now the Nadia district) and much of Bengal. (b) The relations seem to have alternated between friendly and conflictual.
s: Part (a): Nadiya, and much of Bengal
Part (b): alternated between friendly and conflictual

questions.q: After the decline of which dynasty did the Senas emerge as the dominant power over much of Bengal?
questions.a: The Senas rose after the decline of the Palas. The Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas are named in the chapter only as overlords of the Paramaras, and the Eastern Gangas ruled Kalinga.

questions.q:
A history club in Bhubaneswar plans a poster on a dynasty of Kalinga. Its notes say: the dynasty's inscriptions claim a kingdom stretching 'from the Ganga to the Godavari' by the end of the 12th century; it began the great temple of a famous coastal pilgrim town and, later, a grand Sun temple on the Odisha coast; and it had links by marriage with a powerful southern dynasty, though these did not always keep the peace.
(a) Name the dynasty and the two temples.
(b) Name the southern dynasty.
(c) In which century did work on the Sun temple begin, and how does the chapter describe the dynasty's standing among eastern powers by the end of the 12th century?
(d) The club wants a poster line saying the dynasty was 'one of the most stable powers of eastern India'. Which note, the territorial claim or the marriage links, is the stronger support for that line? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) The Eastern Gangas; the Jagannatha temple at Puri and the Sun temple at Konark. (b) The Cholas. (c) The 13th century (mid-13th); one of the most stable powers of eastern India. (d) The territorial claim is stronger: a kingdom said to extend from the Ganga to the Godavari points to a large, lasting state, though the chapter notes it is what their inscriptions claim. The marriage links are weaker support because the same chapter says the dynasty clashed with the Cholas a few times.
s: Part (a): Eastern Gangas, Puri and Konark
Part (b): the Cholas
Part (c): 13th century, and one of the most stable powers
Part (d): picks the territorial claim, with the inscription caveat and why the marriage links are weaker

questions.q: Tara says, 'The Eastern Gangas had marriage alliances with the Cholas and still clashed with them, so in this period a marriage alliance did not by itself keep the peace.' Is her claim supported by the chapter? Answer with the chapter and say how far it can be stretched.
questions.a: Yes, for the cases the chapter gives. The Eastern Gangas had matrimonial alliances with the Cholas yet clashed with them a few times, and the Eastern Chalukyas, drawn into the Chola sphere through marriage alliances, became the object of fierce wars over Vengi. But the chapter gives only these cases, so Tara cannot say that every marriage alliance failed.
s: Verdict: supported by the chapter's cases
Evidence: Eastern Gangas' alliances with the Cholas and their clashes; Vengi wars
Limit: only these cases are given, so no claim about every alliance

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about eastern India and the Deccan.
1. Kalinga corresponds more or less to present-day Assam, which the chapter calls Kamarupa.
2. Inscriptions of the Eastern Gangas claim a kingdom extending from the Ganga to the Godavari.
3. The Eastern Chalukyas were gradually absorbed into the Chola sphere of influence through marriage alliances.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 1 is false: Kamarupa is Assam, while Kalinga is more or less present-day Odisha.

questions.q: (a) Which present-day regions do Kamarupa and Kalinga correspond to, as the chapter gives them? (b) The Western Chalukyas were a major Deccan power: from which capital did they rule, and how far north did their rule extend at some point?
questions.a: (a) Kamarupa is Assam; Kalinga is more or less present-day Odisha. (b) They ruled from Kalyani (Kalyana), and their rule extended at some point to the Narmada River.
s: Part (a): Kamarupa is Assam and Kalinga is more or less Odisha
Part (b): capital Kalyani and the Narmada as the northern limit

questions.q:
A history teacher in Pune writes clues on the board about a Deccan dynasty: 'Its rule extended at some point to the Narmada River. It fought fierce wars with the Cholas over a fertile eastern region. In the end it faded away.' A student then writes in her notebook: 'The Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas defeated this dynasty in battle and ended it.'
(a) Name the dynasty and its capital.
(b) Name the fertile region the wars were fought over and the dynasty that held it before it entered the Chola sphere.
(c) Which two dynasties grew stronger, according to the chapter?
(d) Judge the student's sentence using only what the chapter says, and write a sentence the chapter fully supports.
questions.a: (a) The Western Chalukyas, with their capital at Kalyani (Kalyana). (b) Vengi and the fertile region around it; the Eastern Chalukyas held it before they were gradually absorbed into the Chola sphere. (c) The Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas. (d) The chapter does not say they defeated the Western Chalukyas in battle: it says the fierce wars with the Cholas made the Western Chalukyas fade away while the Kakatiyas and Hoysalas grew stronger and eventually replaced them. A supported sentence: 'After the wars with the Cholas weakened the Western Chalukyas, the Kakatiyas and Hoysalas grew stronger and replaced them.'
s: Part (a): Western Chalukyas, Kalyani
Part (b): Vengi, and the Eastern Chalukyas as its earlier holders
Part (c): Kakatiyas and Hoysalas
Part (d): rejects the unsupported 'defeated in battle' and gives the chapter-based sentence

questions.q: Name the two temples that the Eastern Gangas initiated, and say which of the two was begun in the mid-13th century.
questions.a: The Jagannatha temple at Puri and the grand Sun temple at Konark; the Konark Sun temple was begun in the mid-13th century.
s: Jagannatha temple at Puri and the Sun temple at Konark
Konark as the one begun in the mid-13th century

questions.q: Trace how the wars over Vengi changed the balance of power in the Deccan.
questions.a: The Western Chalukyas ruled from Kalyani and were a major Deccan power, their rule reaching the Narmada at one point. The Eastern Chalukyas, with their capital Vengi, were gradually absorbed into the Chola sphere through marriage alliances. Vengi and the fertile region around it became the object of fierce wars between the Cholas and the Western Chalukyas. As a result the Western Chalukyas faded away. The Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas grew stronger and eventually replaced them.
s: Western Chalukyas as a major Deccan power from Kalyani
Eastern Chalukyas absorbed into the Chola sphere by marriage alliances
Fierce wars over Vengi
Western Chalukyas faded away
Kakatiyas and Hoysalas replaced them

questions.q: A student reads about a Deccan power with its capital at Kalyani, whose rule once reached the Narmada and which fought fierce wars with the Cholas over the fertile region of Vengi. What happened to it in the long run?
questions.a: The wars weakened it and it faded away, with the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas growing stronger and eventually replacing it. The other options reverse who absorbed whom.
o: It faded and was replaced by the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas
It absorbed the Cholas through marriage alliances
It became part of the Chola sphere like the Eastern Chalukyas
It merged with the Senas of Bengal and moved its capital to Nadiya

questions.q: (a) Name the capitals of the Western Chalukyas and of the Eastern Chalukyas. (b) Why did Vengi and its fertile region become the object of fierce wars?
questions.a: (a) Kalyani (Kalyana) for the Western Chalukyas and Vengi for the Eastern Chalukyas. (b) The Eastern Chalukyas were gradually absorbed into the Chola sphere through marriage alliances, so the Cholas and the Western Chalukyas fought over Vengi.
s: Part (a): Kalyani and Vengi
Part (b): Chola sphere after marriage alliances, so Cholas and Western Chalukyas fought for it

questions.q: On a school trip a pilgrim visits the Jagannatha temple at Puri and then the grand Sun temple at Konark. The guide says one dynasty began the construction of both. Which dynasty is it?
questions.a: The chapter credits the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga with initiating both. The Senas ruled Bengal, the Western Chalukyas the Deccan and the Kakatiyas Telangana.

questions.q: A student wrote, 'The stone gateways of the Warangal fort were built by the Hoysalas.' Show with two facts from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Warangal is the modern name of Orugallu, the capital of the Kakatiyas, who built the fort with its stone toranas. The Hoysalas originated in southern Karnataka and had their capitals at Velapura and Dvarasamudra (today's Belur and Halebidu), so they were not the builders of the Warangal fort.
s: Orugallu or Warangal as the Kakatiya capital with the fort and toranas
Hoysala capitals at Velapura and Dvarasamudra
Concludes that the gateways are Kakatiya work

questions.q: (a) Name the Kakatiya capital and one feature of its fort. (b) In which languages did the Kakatiya kings and court show literary interest?
questions.a: (a) Orugallu (Warangal); a fort with impressive stone gateways (toranas). (b) Some kings composed works in Sanskrit, and they patronised Telugu literature.
s: Part (a): Orugallu and stone toranas
Part (b): Sanskrit works by some kings and patronage of Telugu literature

questions.q:
A Hyderabad school plans a heritage walk on a 12th-century dynasty of Telangana. The guide's notes mention the fort at the capital, a famous temple at Hanamkonda, and the dynasty's care for irrigation, village councils and an efficient way to collect revenue. The walk has time for one more stop, either on administration and irrigation or on Telugu and Sanskrit literature. A class poll shows 20 of 30 students are curious about how villages got water and managed local affairs, and 6 about literature.
(a) Name the dynasty and the old name of its capital.
(b) Name the gateways of the fort and the Hanamkonda temple.
(c) A village faces failed rains. Which of the three measures (irrigation, village self-governance, revenue system) would it lean on most, and why?
(d) Using the poll and the chapter, choose the extra stop and justify it.
questions.a: (a) The Kakatiyas; Orugallu (Warangal). (b) Toranas; the Thousand Pillar temple. (c) Irrigation, because it supplies water when rains fail (with village self-governance to organise it); any measure with a reasoned link to the failed rains is acceptable. (d) The administration and irrigation stop: 20 of 30 students want it against 6 for literature, and the chapter shows that these measures supported agricultural prosperity, on which the economy rested.
s: Part (a): Kakatiyas and Orugallu
Part (b): toranas and the Thousand Pillar temple
Part (c): irrigation (or another measure) with a reason tied to failed rains
Part (d): chooses administration and irrigation using 20 of 30 against 6 and the chapter

questions.q: (a) Name two measures by which the Kakatiya rulers supported agriculture and local life. (b) Explain how village self-governance and irrigation together could help a village in a year of poor rain.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: village self-governance, an efficient revenue system, an irrigation infrastructure. (b) For example, irrigation supplies water when the rains are poor, while village self-governance lets the village organise the sharing and upkeep of that water and settle local matters itself, so farming and prosperity are less hit.
s: Part (a): two correct measures
Part (b): links irrigation or local administration to farming in poor-rain years

questions.q: Neha says, 'The Hoysala name legend is proved fact because it is written in inscriptions and shown in temples.' Do you agree? Answer with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter calls it a legend and says the name 'is said to' come from the ascetic's command. It is mentioned in inscriptions and depicted in several temples, which shows it was widely told and recorded, but that does not prove it as fact; the chapter does not present it as proved history.
s: Verdict: does not accept 'proved fact'
The chapter calls it a legend and uses 'is said to'
Inscriptions and temple depictions show the legend was recorded, not that it is proved

questions.q: The Kakatiyas ruled from Orugallu. By what name is this place known today?
questions.a: Orugallu is today's Warangal. Hanamkonda is the place of the Thousand Pillar temple, and Halebidu was a Hoysala capital.

questions.q: The elders of a 12th-century village in Telangana want local problems settled in the village and crops protected from uncertain rains. Which pair of policies of the Kakatiya rulers would help them most?
questions.a: The Kakatiyas promoted village self-governance and developed irrigation infrastructure. Temple architecture and Kannada poetry, sea expeditions and temporary land assignments were not their measures for villagers.
o: Village self-governance and an irrigation infrastructure
Kannada literature and carved temple panels
A naval expedition and merchant guilds

questions.q: Describe the administration and the cultural contributions of the Kakatiyas.
questions.a: In the 12th century they cemented their authority over much of present-day Telangana and Andhra Pradesh from Orugallu (Warangal). They built a fort with stone toranas. Some kings composed Sanskrit works and they patronised Telugu literature. The Thousand Pillar temple at Hanamkonda is a fine example of their architecture. They promoted strong local administration based on village self-governance, an efficient revenue system and an irrigation infrastructure that supported agricultural prosperity.
s: Territory and the capital Orugallu
The fort with stone toranas
Sanskrit works and Telugu literature
The Thousand Pillar temple at Hanamkonda
Village self-governance, revenue system and irrigation

questions.q: Compare the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas on their home regions, capitals, literary patronage, temple legacy and relations with the older powers.
questions.a: The Kakatiyas held much of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh; the Hoysalas began in southern Karnataka. Capitals: Orugallu for the Kakatiyas, Velapura and Dvarasamudra for the Hoysalas. The Kakatiyas patronised Telugu (and Sanskrit) literature, the Hoysalas Kannada. Kakatiya temples include the Thousand Pillar temple; the Hoysalas are known for the carved temples at Belur and Halebidu. Both replaced the Western Chalukyas, and the Hoysalas under Vishnuvardhana broke from Chalukya overlordship and challenged the Cholas.
s: Home regions of both
Capitals of both
Literary patronage: Telugu and Sanskrit versus Kannada
Temple legacy of each
Both grew as the Western Chalukyas faded; Hoysalas broke from Chalukya overlordship

questions.q: (a) In which part of present-day Karnataka did the Hoysalas originate, and over how much of present-day Karnataka did they extend their sway under Vishnuvardhana? (b) In which language did Hoysala rule see cultural and literary development?
questions.a: (a) Southern Karnataka; they gradually extended their sway over most of present-day Karnataka. (b) Kannada.
s: Part (a): southern Karnataka, and later most of present-day Karnataka
Part (b): Kannada

questions.q:
Students from Mysuru visit a Hoysala temple and hear its founding legend: a ruler's ancestor was commanded by an ascetic to act when a tiger appeared. Back in school they plan one wall display. Two ideas are proposed: Display 1, 'Hoysalas, the warriors who broke away from an overlord'; Display 2, 'Hoysalas, the temple builders recognised by UNESCO'. A visitor poll shows that 40 of 50 visitors came mainly to see the carved temples.
(a) What was the command and what does it mean?
(b) Name the two capitals with their present names and say what is recognised by UNESCO there.
(c) Which king broke away from Chalukya overlordship, and whom did he challenge?
(d) Choose one display, justifying it with the poll and one chapter fact about the temples, and say what Display 1 would still need to include.
questions.a: (a) 'Poy, Sala', meaning 'strike, Sala', in old Kannada. (b) Velapura (Belur) and Dvarasamudra (Halebidu); their temples are among three Hoysala temples recognised by UNESCO as world heritage monuments. (c) Vishnuvardhana, who challenged the Cholas. (d) Display 2: 40 of 50 visitors came for the temples, and the chapter calls the intricately carved stone pillars, sculptures and panels their most visible legacy. Display 1 would still need Vishnuvardhana's break from the Chalukyas and challenge to the Cholas.
s: Part (a): Poy, Sala meaning strike, Sala
Part (b): Velapura (Belur), Dvarasamudra (Halebidu), UNESCO recognition of their temples
Part (c): Vishnuvardhana, who challenged the Cholas
Part (d): Display 2 with the poll and a temple fact, noting what Display 1 would add

questions.q: The Kakatiya fort at Orugallu was noted for its impressive stone 'toranas'. What are toranas?
questions.a: The chapter defines toranas as gateways. They are not pillars, irrigation tanks or village councils, which are other parts of the Kakatiya story.

questions.q: Narrate in two or three sentences the legend of how the Hoysalas got their name.
questions.a: Their founder Sala went to a Jain temple and found an ascetic meditating when a tiger appeared. The ascetic said 'Poy, Sala' (strike, Sala) in old Kannada; Sala obeyed and saved his life, and the ascetic blessed him with kingship.
s: Sala at the Jain temple, the ascetic and the tiger
The command 'Poy, Sala', Sala's obedience and the blessing of kingship

questions.q: On a school trip near Mysuru, Meera sees a temple with numerous elaborate statues, friezes at the bottom and intricately carved pillars. Which style does it belong to?
questions.a: This is the Hoysala style, as at Belur and Halebidu. The Thousand Pillar temple is Kakatiya, the Brihadishvara temple is Chola and Kandariya Mahadeva is Chandella.
o: Hoysala style, like the temples at Belur and Halebidu
Kakatiya style, like the Thousand Pillar temple at Hanamkonda
Chola style, like the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur
Chandella style, like the Kandariya Mahadeva temple

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The temples at Belur and Halebidu are recognised by UNESCO as world heritage monuments.
Reason (R): Hoysala rule saw cultural and literary development in the Kannada language.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the Kannada literary development does not explain the UNESCO recognition. The chapter ties the monuments to the Hoysalas' unique temple architecture with intricately carved pillars, sculptures and panels.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: What is the 'most visible legacy' of the Hoysalas according to the chapter? Describe two features of it.
questions.a: Their unique style of temple architecture. Features: intricately carved stone pillars, sculptures and panels, as at Belur and Halebidu.
s: Names the temple architecture as the legacy
Two features: carved stone pillars, sculptures, panels

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a Kakatiya achievement described in the chapter?
questions.a: The temples at Belur and Halebidu belong to the Hoysalas. The Kakatiyas are credited with the Thousand Pillar temple at Hanamkonda, an efficient revenue system and irrigation.
o: Building the temples at Belur and Halebidu
Building the Thousand Pillar temple at Hanamkonda

questions.q: In the legend of the Hoysala name, the ascetic said 'Poy, Sala' when a tiger appeared. What do these words mean in old Kannada?
questions.a: The chapter says 'Poy, Sala' means 'strike, Sala', and Sala obeyed and saved the ascetic's life. The other verbs are not given.

questions.q:
Read these statements about the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas.
1. The Kakatiyas promoted village self-governance, an efficient revenue system and irrigation.
2. The capitals of the Hoysalas were Orugallu and Hanamkonda.
3. Under Vishnuvardhana the Hoysalas stayed loyal to the Chalukya overlords and avoided the Cholas.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 1 is from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: Orugallu was Kakatiya, and the Hoysala capitals were Velapura and Dvarasamudra. Statement 3 is false: under Vishnuvardhana they broke away from Chalukya overlordship and challenged the Cholas.

questions.q: The chapter says the Western Chalukyas faded while the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas grew stronger. Describe what the chapter says happened, and what Vishnuvardhana did to extend the Hoysalas' power.
questions.a: The wars with the Cholas over Vengi made the Western Chalukyas fade away, while the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas grew stronger and eventually replaced them. Under Vishnuvardhana the Hoysalas broke away from Chalukya overlordship, challenged the Cholas and gradually extended their sway over most of present-day Karnataka.
s: Western Chalukyas faded because of the wars with the Cholas
Hoysalas broke from Chalukya overlordship and challenged the Cholas
Extended control over most of present-day Karnataka

questions.q: Compare Rajaraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I in terms of their reigns, conquests, monuments and other deeds.
questions.a: Rajaraja ruled from 985 for about three decades; Rajendra I ruled for nearly 30 years. Rajaraja conquered parts of Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, the Maldives and northern Sri Lanka; Rajendra conquered parts of Odisha and Bengal and expanded the conquest of northern Sri Lanka. Rajaraja built the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur; Rajendra built a temple at Gangaikondacholapuram. Rajaraja facilitated a Buddhist vihara at Nagapattinam; Rajendra took the title Gangaikondachola and led the 1025 naval expedition against Srivijaya.
s: The length of both reigns
Conquests of Rajaraja
Conquests of Rajendra
The monument of each king
One further distinct deed of each king

questions.q:
A Madurai school's history fair has a stall with three cards. Card 1 reads: 'In 985 a king began a rule of about three decades.' Card 2: 'His son took the throne in 1014; in 1025 his navy sailed across the Bay of Bengal.' Card 3: 'Two great temples remember the two kings.' The stall head wants the title 'Conquerors of the Sea' and a fourth card saying 'The son conquered and occupied the Srivijaya Empire.'
(a) Name the two kings and the temples the third card refers to.
(b) Name the kingdom the fleet defeated and say how many years after the son's accession it sailed.
(c) State two reasons for the expedition.
(d) Judge the stall head's fourth card using the chapter, and say whether the title 'Conquerors of the Sea' can still be defended.
questions.a: (a) Rajaraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I; the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur and the temple at Gangaikondacholapuram. (b) Srivijaya; 1025 minus 1014 = 11 years after his accession. (c) Competition over the Strait of Malacca on the China trade route, and the thriving maritime trade with China. (d) The card is wrong: the fleet defeated the Srivijaya forces and captured their capital, but Rajendra did not try to occupy the empire; it was a punitive expedition. The title can still be defended by the naval victory, the Maldives and Sri Lanka conquests, but the word 'occupied' must go.
s: Part (a): the two kings and their two temples
Part (b): Srivijaya, and 11 years after accession
Part (c): two correct reasons from the trade rivalry
Part (d): rejects 'occupied' (punitive, no occupation) and defends the title on the naval victory

questions.q:
Match each person in Column A with the deed in Column B.
Column A: 1. Rajaraja Chola I  2. Rajendra Chola I  3. Vijayabahu I of Sri Lanka  4. The Srivijaya ruler
Column B: a. drove the Cholas out of Sri Lanka  b. made donations to Nalanda  c. led a navy against Srivijaya  d. built the Brihadishvara temple
questions.a: Rajaraja built the Brihadishvara temple, Rajendra sent the navy against Srivijaya, Vijayabahu I drove the Cholas out of Sri Lanka and the Srivijaya ruler made donations to Nalanda. The wrong options swap the two Chola kings or the two island rulers.

questions.q: A merchant guild at the Chola port of Nagapattinam hears in the 1020s that the king's fleet will punish a kingdom across the Bay of Bengal that holds a narrow sea route on the China trade. Which kingdom is meant?
questions.a: The Srivijaya king controlled the Strait of Malacca, on a sea route to China. Anuradhapura, the Pandyas and the Western Chalukyas were Chola rivals but not across the bay on that route.
o: Srivijaya, which held the Strait of Malacca
The Pandyas, who later absorbed the Chola empire
The Western Chalukyas, who fought over Vengi

questions.q: (a) Name the three capital cities of the Cholas with their present-day names. (b) Which Chola king built a temple at Gangaikondacholapuram, and what does it commemorate?
questions.a: (a) Tanjavur (Thanjavur), Gangaikondacholapuram and Kanchi (Kanchipuram). (b) Rajendra Chola I; his victory over north Indian rulers.
s: Part (a): Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram, Kanchipuram
Part (b): Rajendra I, victory over north Indian rulers

questions.q: A tourist in Nagapattinam learns that a Buddhist vihara once stood in this port of a mostly Shaivite empire. How does the chapter explain it?
questions.a: Rajaraja facilitated its construction for the ruler of the Srivijaya Empire. The other options attach the vihara to Rajendra's victory memorial, to Nalanda's monastery land or to Sri Lanka's Vijayabahu.
o: Rajaraja facilitated a vihara built for the Srivijaya ruler
Rajendra built it to celebrate his victory over north Indian rulers
A Pala king granted land for it as at Nalanda
Vijayabahu I built it after driving the Cholas out

questions.q: Kavya says, 'Rajendra's attack on Srivijaya proves that India and Southeast Asia were mostly enemies.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter calls the expedition a punitive one over trade competition, and it did not seek to occupy the defeated empire. It also says relations were deep, cultural and generally peaceful, with a Srivijaya ruler making donations to Nalanda and being granted land for a monastery, and a Buddhist vihara at Nagapattinam.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'mostly enemies'
The expedition was punitive over trade competition, with no occupation
Evidence of peaceful links: Nalanda monastery or the Nagapattinam vihara

questions.q: (a) Which Chola king claimed the conquest of the 'islands of the sea', and what do most historians identify them with? (b) Which part of Sri Lanka did he conquer, and which kingdom was included?
questions.a: (a) Rajaraja Chola; the Maldives. (b) The northern part of Sri Lanka, including the kingdom of Anuradhapura.
s: Part (a): Rajaraja, the Maldives
Part (b): northern Sri Lanka and Anuradhapura

questions.q: Priya writes in her notebook, 'Rajendra Chola I ruled from 985 to 1014, and his father Rajaraja from 1014 to 1044.' Using the dates in the chapter, show that this cannot be right, and give the correct reigns with their lengths.
questions.a: The chapter says Rajaraja ruled from 985 and his son Rajendra from 1014 to 1044. So the order is reversed: Rajaraja ruled 985 to 1014, which is 29 years ('some three decades'), and Rajendra 1014 to 1044, which is 30 years ('nearly 30 years').
s: States that Rajaraja ruled from 985 and Rajendra, his son, from 1014, so the notebook order is impossible
Correct reign of Rajaraja, 985 to 1014, which is 29 years
Correct reign of Rajendra, 1014 to 1044, which is 30 years

questions.q: What does the title 'Gangaikondachola', taken by Rajendra Chola I, mean?
questions.a: It means 'the Chola who seized (or brought) Ganga', a reference to his northern campaigns and the sacredness of the Ganga. The other options give titles or deeds that belong to different events.
o: The Chola who seized or brought Ganga
The Chola who ruled the islands of the sea
The Chola who built the great temple at Thanjavur
The Chola who captured the Srivijaya capital

questions.q: 'The Cholas were masters of the seas.' Justify this statement using five points from the chapter.
questions.a: Rajaraja conquered the 'islands of the sea', identified with the Maldives, and northern Sri Lanka. Under the Cholas trade with China thrived and Rajendra sent a diplomatic mission there. Nagapattinam was an important port. The Strait of Malacca on the China route was controlled by the Srivijaya king, so in 1025 Rajendra sent his navy, which defeated the Srivijaya forces and captured their capital. It was a punitive expedition supported by many Indian merchant guilds, and he did not occupy the empire.
s: Island conquests: the Maldives and northern Sri Lanka
Thriving trade with China and the diplomatic mission
The Strait of Malacca and the cause of the expedition
The 1025 expedition: forces defeated, capital captured
Punitive in nature, supported by merchant guilds, no occupation

questions.q: Explain how the Cholas' wars contributed to the decline of their empire, and say what finally happened to the empire.
questions.a: Frequent and extensive conflicts with several neighbouring kingdoms, in particular the Western Chalukyas, the Pandyas and the rulers of Sri Lanka, drained the Chola treasury and contributed to the decline. By the 13th century the empire had shrunk considerably, and it was finally absorbed by the Pandyas.
s: Names the neighbours: Western Chalukyas, Pandyas and Sri Lankan rulers
Frequent and extensive wars drained the treasury and contributed to the decline
Shrank by the 13th century and was finally absorbed by the Pandyas

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the public works of the Cholas?
questions.a: The Cholas built roads, tanks, wells, canals and artificial lakes. Forts with stone gateways were a Kakatiya feature at Orugallu.
o: Tanks, wells and canals for irrigation

questions.q: The chapter warns us not to conclude from Rajendra's expedition that India and the Srivijaya Empire were hostile. Give the chapter's reason and one example.
questions.a: There were deep cultural and generally peaceful relations between the two regions. For example, a Srivijaya ruler made donations to Nalanda and asked the Pala king for land to create one more monastery there, and the request was granted.
s: Reason: deep cultural and generally peaceful relations
Example: the Srivijaya ruler's donations and monastery at Nalanda

questions.q:
A Chennai school builds a wall timeline on the Cholas and Sri Lanka. Card 1: 'A king who began to rule in 985 conquered the northern part of the island.' Card 2: 'His son expanded the conquest, and the region stayed in the empire for a long spell.' Card 3: 'A Sri Lankan king freed the island from the Cholas in a single battle.'
(a) Name the two Chola kings and the kingdom of northern Sri Lanka that was included in the conquest.
(b) For about how long did northern Sri Lanka remain an integral part of the Chola Empire?
(c) Name the Sri Lankan king who ended it and one family link with India that the chapter mentions for him.
(d) Judge Card 3 using the chapter and rewrite it.
questions.a: (a) Rajaraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I; the kingdom of Anuradhapura. (b) Half a century or so. (c) Vijayabahu I; he married a princess from Kalinga. (d) Card 3 is wrong: the chapter says Vijayabahu I managed to drive the Cholas out after several battles, not one. A supported card: 'After several battles, the Sri Lankan king Vijayabahu I drove the Cholas out after about half a century of Chola hold.'
s: Part (a): Rajaraja, Rajendra and Anuradhapura
Part (b): about half a century
Part (c): Vijayabahu I and his marriage to a Kalinga princess
Part (d): rejects 'single battle', cites several battles and rewrites the card

questions.q: Give two pieces of evidence or actions from the chapter that show trade with China thrived under the Cholas.
questions.a: Archaeological evidence and inscriptions confirm that trade relations with China thrived, and Rajendra even sent a diplomatic mission to China.
s: Archaeological evidence and inscriptions confirm thriving trade
Rajendra's diplomatic mission to China

questions.q: (a) Which present-day regions in the north did Rajendra Chola I conquer? (b) How was Rajendra related to Rajaraja Chola I?
questions.a: (a) Parts of present-day Odisha and Bengal. (b) He was Rajaraja's son.
s: Part (a): parts of Odisha and Bengal
Part (b): Rajaraja's son

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rajendra Chola I sent his navy against the king of the Srivijaya Empire.
Reason (R): The Srivijaya king controlled the Strait of Malacca, on one of the sea routes in the maritime trade with China, and this created competition with the Cholas.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the competition over the Strait of Malacca and the China trade is the cause the chapter gives for the expedition, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Cholas.
1. Rajaraja Chola conquered parts of Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh and the 'islands of the sea', which most historians identify with the Maldives.
2. Rajendra's navy captured the Srivijaya capital, but he did not try to occupy the defeated empire.
3. The Cholas held northern Sri Lanka without a break until the 13th century.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 is false: northern Sri Lanka was part of the Chola Empire for half a century or so, until Vijayabahu I drove them out.

questions.q: Rajaraja Chola built a temple at Thanjavur that is also called Rajarajeshwaram. What is its other name?
questions.a: It is the Brihadishvara temple. The Bhojeshwar temple belongs to the Paramaras, the Kandariya Mahadeva to the Chandellas and the Jagannatha temple to the Eastern Gangas.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Bhojeshwar temple was completed during Bhoja's lifetime.
Reason (R): The Bhojeshwar temple remains an architectural marvel even though it was never completed.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The assertion is false, because the chapter says the temple was never completed. The reason is true: it still stands as a marvel.
o: A is false, but R is true.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: State two differences between Bhoja Paramara and King Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty.
questions.a: The Paramara Bhoja ruled from 1010 for almost half a century from Dhara in Malwa. The Pratihara Bhoja lived in the 9th century and belonged to the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, met in the previous chapter.
s: Period: 1010 for the Paramara, the 9th century for the Pratihara
Dynasty and region: Paramara of Malwa, Gurjara-Pratihara for the other

questions.q: Explain how the lake of Bhoja was useful to the kingdom and how it is remembered today.
questions.a: It was vast, built by harnessing the waters of several rivers between Bhojpur and Bhopal. It served irrigation and water management. It is remembered through the surviving portion Bhojtal, the remains of embankments, the name Bhopal from Bhojpal and the Hindi proverb.
s: Size: vast, from the waters of several rivers
Uses: irrigation and water management
Memory: Bhojtal, embankments, the name Bhopal or the proverb

questions.q: Assess the reign of Bhoja Paramara under these heads: length and conquests, help to others, public works, and what happened after his death.
questions.a: He ruled from 1010 for almost half a century, until 1055, and led numerous campaigns that extended the kingdom from the Konkan to parts of Rajasthan. He sent forces to help the Hindu Shahis against Mahmud of Ghazni. He founded Bhojpur, built a vast lake by harnessing several rivers and began the Bhojeshwar temple, which was never completed. After his death in 1055 the Paramaras gradually declined, partly because of conflicts with neighbouring powers.
s: Length of reign, 1010 to 1055
Campaigns from the Konkan to parts of Rajasthan
Help sent to the Hindu Shahis against Mahmud
Bhojpur, the vast lake and the unfinished Bhojeshwar temple
Decline after 1055 partly through conflicts with neighbours

questions.q: 'Bhoja Paramara was a scholar as well as a king.' Justify this statement with five points from the chapter.
questions.a: He was a generous patron who supported scholars and promoted Sanskrit literature, so arts and sciences flourished and his capital became a renowned centre of learning. He himself wrote Samarangana Sutradhara on architecture, town planning, temple construction, sculpture and mechanical devices, treatises on governance and Sanskrit poetics, a commentary on Patanjali's Yogasutras and texts of medicine. His reputation as a wise and learned ruler became legendary, inspiring stories and folk tales.
s: Patron of scholars and Sanskrit literature
His capital as a renowned centre of learning
Samarangana Sutradhara and its subjects
Governance, poetics, Yogasutras commentary and medicine
Legendary reputation in stories and folk tales

questions.q: From which word does the name of the city of Bhopal come, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says Bhopal comes from 'Bhojpal', the dam or fort of Bhoja. Bhojtal is the surviving part of the lake, Bhojpur is a town he founded and Bhojeshwar is his temple.

questions.q:
Study the following statements about the Paramaras.
1. The Paramaras were always independent rulers of Malwa.
2. Bhoja's reign lasted only about twenty years.
3. Bhoja was among the Indian rulers who sent forces to help the Hindu Shahis against Mahmud.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 3 is true. Statement 1 is false: the Paramaras were originally vassals of the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas. Statement 2 is false: Bhoja ruled from 1010 for almost half a century, until 1055.

questions.q: Sunita says, 'The Bhoja of Malwa and the Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty are the same king, since both are called Bhoja.' Do you agree? Argue from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says Bhoja Paramara should not be confused with Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty. The Paramara Bhoja ruled from 1010 in Malwa, with Dhara as capital, while the Pratihara Bhoja lived in the 9th century. A shared name does not make one person.
s: Verdict: they are different kings
The Paramara Bhoja: from 1010, Malwa, Dhara
The Pratihara Bhoja: 9th century, a different dynasty

questions.q:
A school librarian shelves a book on a medieval king who wrote a long treatise on town planning, temple construction and mechanical devices, a work on governance, a commentary on an ancient yoga text and texts on medicine. A parent objects: 'These stories about a wise, learned king are just legends and should not be taught.'
(a) Name the king and the treatise on town planning.
(b) Name the ancient yoga text and its author.
(c) Name two pieces of lasting evidence of his public works that the chapter mentions.
(d) Judge the parent's objection using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Bhoja Paramara; Samarangana Sutradhara. (b) The Yogasutras of Patanjali. (c) Any two of: Bhojtal, the remains of the embankments of the vast lake, the town of Bhojpur. (d) Partly right: the chapter says his reputation became legendary and inspired folk tales. But the chapter also gives lasting evidence from his rule and works attributed to him, so the facts of his rule, works and public works are worth teaching, while the folk tales can be marked as stories.
s: Part (a): Bhoja Paramara and Samarangana Sutradhara
Part (b): Yogasutras by Patanjali
Part (c): two surviving remains of his public works
Part (d): balanced judgement separating legend from the chapter's evidence

questions.q: Which of the following is a long treatise by Bhoja on architecture, town planning, temple construction, sculpture and mechanical devices?
questions.a: Samarangana Sutradhara is the treatise by Bhoja. Manasollasa is the encyclopaedia of Someshvara III, Gitagovindam is Jayadeva's poem and Lilavati is Bhaskaracharya's work.
o: Manasollasa, the encyclopaedia of Someshvara III

questions.q: A boy in Bhopal sees long earthen and stone embankments in fields far away from the small lake near the city and asks what they are. What does the chapter suggest?
questions.a: They are remains of the vast lake Bhoja built by harnessing the waters of several rivers, of which only Bhojtal now remains. The other options give works of other rulers.
o: Remains of Bhoja's lake built from several rivers
Remains of canals the Cholas built to irrigate the fields
Remains of the walls of the Kakatiya fort at Orugallu
Remains of a dam built by the Hoysalas at Belur

questions.q: A quiz card describes a king whose numerous campaigns extended his kingdom from a region on the west coast to parts of Rajasthan. Which king and region does the card describe, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Bhoja Paramara extended his kingdom from the Konkan region on the west coast to parts of Rajasthan. The other options attach other kings and regions of the chapter to the description.
o: Bhoja Paramara, from the Konkan region
Rajaraja Chola, from the coast of Karnataka
The Eastern Gangas, from the Ganga to the Godavari
The Kakatiyas, from Orugallu to Hanamkonda

questions.q: A quiz-master has three answer cards: '1055', 'Dhara' and 'Bhojtal'. Write one question for each so that the card is the only correct answer, using facts from the chapter.
questions.a: For example: In which year did Bhoja die? (1055). Which city was the Paramara capital? (Dhara). Which part of Bhoja's vast lake still remains near Bhopal? (Bhojtal).
s: A correct question that has 1055 as its only answer
A correct question that has Dhara as its only answer
A correct question that has Bhojtal as its only answer

questions.q: How did Bhoja's patronage change his capital?
questions.a: He supported scholars and promoted Sanskrit literature, and under him arts and sciences flourished. His capital became a renowned centre of learning that attracted scholars, poets and artists from across India.
s: Supported scholars and Sanskrit literature, arts and sciences flourished
The capital became a renowned centre of learning drawing people from across India

questions.q: (a) Whose vassals were the Paramaras at first? (b) When and where did they become an independent power, and what was their capital?
questions.a: (a) Of the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas. (b) In the second half of the 10th century, in Malwa (in present-day Madhya Pradesh), with Dhara (Dhar) as capital.
s: Part (a): vassals of the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas
Part (b): second half of the 10th century, Malwa, capital Dhara

questions.q: (a) For what purposes did the lake built by Bhoja serve? (b) What survives of it today, and what does the Hindi proverb say about it?
questions.a: (a) Irrigation and water management. (b) A small portion, Bhojtal, near Bhopal, with embankments seen further away; the proverb says that if there is a lake, it is Bhopal's lake, and all others are just ponds.
s: Part (a): irrigation and water management
Part (b): Bhojtal survives, and the proverb praises the lake as the one true lake

questions.q: Which city was the capital of the Paramaras of Malwa?
questions.a: The Paramara capital was Dhara (present-day Dhar). Bhojpur was founded by Bhoja, Bhopal is named from Bhojpal, and Ajayameru was the Chahamana capital.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of Bhoja Paramara?
questions.a: Bhoja Paramara ruled from 1010 and should not be confused with Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, who lived in the 9th century. The other three are in the chapter.
o: He was a Gurjara-Pratihara king of the 9th century
He sent forces to help the Hindu Shahis against Mahmud
He built the Bhojeshwar temple, which was never completed
He wrote a commentary on Patanjali's Yogasutras

questions.q: (a) In which year did Bhoja die, and what happened to the Paramaras afterwards? (b) What did the chapter give as a partial cause of that decline?
questions.a: (a) 1055; the Paramaras gradually declined. (b) Conflicts with neighbouring powers.
s: Part (a): died in 1055 and the Paramaras gradually declined
Part (b): partly because of conflicts with neighbouring powers

questions.q:
A Bhopal school takes Class 7 to the lakeside, where a modern statue of a king stands. The guide tells them that the small lake before them is only a part of something much larger, built about a thousand years ago, and that the king ruled from 1010 until his death in 1055. The committee can put up one plaque on the bank of the lake: one on the king as a builder of the lake, or one on the king as a scholar and author.
(a) Name the king and the part of the lake that remains.
(b) Name his dynasty and say whom his forces went to assist against Mahmud of Ghazni.
(c) What does the name of the city Bhopal come from, and what does the Hindi proverb say?
(d) Choose the plaque for this spot and justify it with two facts; say where the other plaque would fit better.
questions.a: (a) Bhoja Paramara; Bhojtal. (b) The Paramaras; the Hindu Shahi rulers. (c) 'Bhojpal', the dam or fort of Bhoja; the proverb says that if there is a lake it is Bhopal's lake and all others are just ponds. (d) The builder plaque suits the lakeside: the vast lake from the waters of several rivers served irrigation and water management, and Bhojtal and the embankments can still be seen. The scholar plaque (Samarangana Sutradhara, the Yogasutras commentary, the capital as a centre of learning) would fit better in a library or school hall.
s: Part (a): Bhoja Paramara and Bhojtal
Part (b): the Paramaras, and the Hindu Shahi rulers
Part (c): Bhojpal and the proverb
Part (d): builder plaque with two lake facts, and where the scholar plaque would fit

questions.q: Describe three ways in which the attack on Nalanda affected learning, using the details the chapter gives.
questions.a: Its famous library, spread over three multi-storey buildings with lakhs of manuscripts, is said to have burned for months. Tibetan scholars teaching and studying there fled to Tibet with as many manuscripts as they could carry. About three decades later it was half ruined, with an old teacher instructing perhaps its last class of about 70 students. Historians also agree the destruction of such centres hastened Buddhism's decline.
s: The library burned for months
Tibetan scholars fled with manuscripts
Half ruined three decades later, perhaps its last class, and Buddhism's decline

questions.q: (a) In which years were the two Battles of Tarain fought, and who won each? (b) How long after the first battle did Muhammad return, and what did he do to Prithviraj III?
questions.a: (a) 1191, won by Prithviraj III, and 1192, won by Muhammad Ghuri. (b) Within a year, with a larger army; in the second battle he defeated and executed Prithviraj III.
s: Part (a): 1191 Prithviraj III, 1192 Muhammad Ghuri
Part (b): returned within a year with a larger army and executed Prithviraj

questions.q: Meena says, 'Muhammad Ghuri won every battle he fought against Indian rulers.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. In 1178 he was defeated by the Chaulukya king Mularaja II at the foot of Mount Abu, and in 1191 Prithviraj III defeated him at Tarain. He won the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192. 'Every' is too strong.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'every'
Defeat at Mount Abu in 1178
Defeat at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191, with the win only in 1192

questions.q: (a) Who was Bakhtiyar Khilji in relation to Qutb-ud-din Aibak? (b) Which regions did he conquer, and which two Buddhist centres did he destroy on the way?
questions.a: (a) Aibak's army commander. (b) Bihar and Bengal; the monasteries and universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila.
s: Part (a): army commander of Aibak
Part (b): Bihar and Bengal; Nalanda and Vikramashila

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the chapter about Nalanda?
